sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.markdown:
**No general, residential, or home-improvement contractor license exists in Maine, and no license covers chimney *sweeping*. But chimney *installation* work tied to fuel-burning heating equipment IS licensed.** The **Maine Fuel Board** licenses Master, Journeyman and Apprentice **Oil Burner and/or Solid Fuel Technicians**, Propane & Natural Gas Technicians, and Limited Wood Pellet Technicians. **32 M.R.S. § 18102** requires a license for "a person who installs or services solid fuel burning equipment, including pellet-fired central heating appliances, or oil, propane or natural gas burning equipment"; **§ 18101** defines "equipment installations" as "the installation, alteration or repair of oil, solid fuel, propane or natural gas burning equipment **and chimneys**, or pellet-fired central heating appliances, including accessory equipment as relating only to the safety of the installation." **§ 18104 exceptions** matter for hearth work: (a) "solid fuel burning fireplace stoves, room heaters and stoves designed exclusively for heating and cooking and not attached to a central heating system" are excepted, and (b) a person making an installation in a single-family residence they occupy as their own abode is excepted (installation must still conform to Board rules). Practical reading: **a freestanding wood stove or fireplace stove install, a masonry repair, or a sweep needs no state license; installing or altering a wood/pellet/oil/gas central-heating appliance and its chimney/liner does** (scope of "chimneys" for a stand-alone liner job not tested by Board guidance — flag, don't overstate). Licensee lookup: Maine Office of Professional & Occupational Regulation (Fuel Board). Electricians and plumbers are also licensed.

For *contracting* generally, the state imposes a contract statute, not a credential: the **Home Construction Contracts Act, 10 M.R.S. chapter 219-A**. **10 M.R.S. § 1487** (verified): "Any home construction contract for more than $3,000 in materials or labor must be in writing" and must include the parties' names/addresses/phones, property location, estimated start and substantial-completion dates, total contract price, method of payment **with the initial down payment limited to no more than 1/3 of the total contract price**, a general description of work and materials, the statutory warranty language, a choice of dispute-resolution method (binding arbitration, nonbinding arbitration, or mediation), a written change-order clause, door-to-door and insulation disclosures where applicable, an energy-standards statement, and the Attorney General's home-construction information/website notice. **Licensing bills keep failing: LD 1226 (2025–26), "An Act to Protect Consumers by Licensing Residential Building Contractors," passed both chambers in June 2025 but sat on the Special Appropriations Table and died when the Legislature adjourned sine die Apr 29, 2026** (REF: LegiScan; WGME). "Licensed and bonded" in Maine typically means a Fuel Board, electrical or plumbing license — never a general chimney credential.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: Wide for sweeping and masonry. Statewide there is **nothing to verify for chimney inspection or masonry competence** beyond a written contract over $3,000 — no exam, no registry. The Fuel Board license tests fuel-appliance installation, not flue diagnosis or NFPA 211 inspection levels, and it excludes freestanding stoves. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) and an independent audit fill the gap.

sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.markdown: **Maine has one of the most chimney-specific seller-disclosure statutes in the country.** **33 M.R.S. § 173** requires the seller of residential property to deliver a written **Property Disclosure Statement**, and its **heating subsection (§ 173(2-A))** requires disclosure of "the date of the most recent inspection of the chimneys and vents for the heating system or source" — language added by **PL 2019, c. 37** (further amended PL 2023, c. 585). That is a chimney line item written into the statute itself. Standard is known-condition: under **33 M.R.S. § 176(1)** "the seller is not obligated under this subchapter to make any specific investigation or inquiry," and the statement is not a warranty. **33 M.R.S. § 174**: if the statement is delivered after the buyer's offer, the buyer may terminate the contract or withdraw the offer **within 72 hours after receipt**, without penalty and with the deposit promptly returned. No inspection is mandated at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: The **Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act (MUTPA), 5 M.R.S. § 207**, is enforced by the AG and privately. **5 M.R.S. § 213**: a consumer who suffers a loss of money or property may recover actual damages, restitution and equitable relief, and **shall be awarded reasonable attorney's fees and costs** if a violation is found; a **written demand for relief must be sent at least 30 days before suit**. Door-to-door and telephone sales fall under the **Consumer Solicitation Sales law, 32 M.R.S. §§ 4661–4671**: **§ 4664** lets the consumer avoid the contract "by giving written notice of avoidance to the seller … within 3 full business days following the day on which the contract or sale was made"; **§ 4664-A** bars the seller from starting work that permanently affixes goods to the home while the cancellation right runs; § 4662 requires a written contract stating the right. That is the exact mechanic against chimney scare-sales. Complaints: Maine AG Consumer Protection Division.

sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.markdown: Maine's statewide code is the **Maine Uniform Building and Energy Code (MUBEC)**, now the **2021 IRC, 2021 IBC and 2021 IECC**, which municipalities that enforce MUBEC must enforce **as of April 7, 2025** (Office of State Fire Marshal). **Municipalities with 4,000+ residents must enforce MUBEC; smaller towns may adopt and enforce it by local action**, so many small/rural towns have **no building code enforcement or permitting**. Where a code and code-enforcement officer exist, chimney relines, rebuilds, crowns, and solid-fuel appliance installs are generally permit work; routine sweeps and like-for-like caps generally are not. Independently of local permits, Fuel Board installation rules apply statewide to licensed equipment installations. This state needs the local-variance disclaimer as much as any.

sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.markdown: **25 M.R.S. § 2468** requires "at least one approved carbon monoxide detector in each area within, or giving access to, bedrooms" in single-family dwellings and covered buildings. **At sale:** a person who acquires a single-family dwelling by sale or exchange must install CO detectors "within 30 days of acquisition or occupancy of the dwelling, whichever is later, if carbon monoxide detectors are not already present," and **the purchaser "shall certify at the closing of the transaction that the purchaser will make the proper installation," a certification "signed and dated by the purchaser."** Landlords must provide working CO detectors at each occupancy. Violation is a civil violation with a fine of up to $500 per violation (waivable if corrected within 10 days). A genuine **CO-at-sale certification** — but the promise runs from the buyer, which makes a buyer-side chimney/stove inspection at transfer the natural pairing.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: Maine has among the **highest wood/pellet-heat shares in the nation**, so solid-fuel practice carries the content weight. No statewide burn-ban regime; federal EPA new-stove emission standards apply (NATIONAL STANDARD). Fuel Board rules govern licensed central solid-fuel and pellet installations (§1). Some towns regulate outdoor wood boilers — **name the local ordinance per listing town; VERIFY.**

sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: The Maine AG's Consumer Protection Division publishes door-to-door sales guidance (maine.gov/ag, "Door-to-Door Sales") and pursues home-construction fraud; the door-knock "we were in the area / noticed your chimney" pitch is a textbook Consumer Solicitation Sales + MUTPA problem. **Specific ME chimney-sweep enforcement actions: NOT FOUND.** Use pattern language only.

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: Maine **CONFIRMS the master correlation, and is the sharpest example in this batch.** It licenses no sweep, no chimney inspector and no general contractor — only the technicians who hook fuel-burning central heating equipment to a chimney — yet its seller-disclosure statute is the most chimney-specific of any launch state: **33 M.R.S. § 173 orders the seller to disclose the date the chimneys and vents were last inspected, in the statute's own words.** Add a buyer's CO-detector certification at closing, a 1/3 down-payment cap on home-construction contracts, and a 3-day door-to-door cancel, and Maine front-loads its protection onto the transaction, not onto any credential. A 2025–26 bill to license residential contractors passed both chambers and still died for lack of funding. The oddball that earns the page: the state literally asks the seller when the flue was last looked at, which is exactly the question this site helps buyers ask.
